readings.title: Speaking practice after work
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
An evening language class attracted adults after work. Many learners knew vocabulary but rarely spoke during the crowded first hour. The main obstacle was speaking time concentrated among confident learners. Long whole-class questions left quieter students without a chance to practise. At first, the people involved did not agree on which part of the proposal deserved the most attention.

To investigate, the team used a record of participation during lessons. The tutor counted speaking turns and asked students which activities felt manageable. The organizers kept the first stage small enough to change without wasting substantial time or resources.

The evidence indicated paired tasks increased active practice. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced short rotating conversations before group discussion. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. The records were useful because they described ordinary use rather than an ideal situation imagined at a meeting.

The case suggests a broader point: confidence grows through repeated opportunities. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The group published its reasons so that people who preferred a different result could still understand the choice. For those taking part in speaking practice after work, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Choosing a reading level
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A library offered graded readers to adult learners. Borrowers often selected books by cover and returned them unfinished. The main obstacle was book levels hidden behind unfamiliar codes. Readers could not tell whether a title matched their vocabulary and reading time. The question mattered to people with different schedules and levels of experience, so one account could not represent everyone.

To investigate, the team used a trial shelf with sample pages. Librarians asked learners to read a short excerpt and explain how they chose a book. A simple record of what happened each day gave the team a starting point for comparison.

The evidence indicated visible samples made levels easier to judge. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced plain-language labels and a range of short extracts. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Some participants welcomed the change immediately, while others noticed practical details that needed further work.

The case suggests a broader point: the right challenge encourages independent reading. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The result was a revised plan, not a claim that every difficulty had disappeared. For those taking part in choosing a reading level, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Listening practice on a bus journey
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
An adult education centre sent listening exercises to phones. Learners liked studying on the bus but found each recording too long. The main obstacle was activities longer than common travel breaks. A single exercise took nearly half an hour and was hard to resume after an interruption. The initial idea sounded reasonable, yet the details of the place made it harder to carry out than expected.

To investigate, the team used learning diaries from commuters. Tutors compared travel times with the points where learners stopped listening. Instead of relying on a single opinion, the team invited several users to describe what they actually did.

The evidence indicated short segments fit real schedules better. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced brief recordings with a clear restart point. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. This allowed the organizers to separate a temporary inconvenience from a pattern that required attention.

The case suggests a broader point: learning materials should fit ordinary lives. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. They also decided when to check the arrangement again, because conditions could change over time. For those taking part in listening practice on a bus journey, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Feedback on a first essay
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
An adult writing class returned essays covered with corrections. Students saw many marks but were unsure which skill to practise next. The main obstacle was feedback without clear priorities. The same page contained notes on ideas, structure, spelling and punctuation. The people affected were invited to comment before a permanent arrangement was chosen.

To investigate, the team used student interviews after the next draft. The teacher asked learners which comment they had acted on and why. The first trial produced both useful results and questions the team could not yet answer.

The evidence indicated two focused suggestions led to stronger revisions. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a short priority note and examples of improvement. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Rather than hide those limits, the public note explained how the next version had been selected.

The case suggests a broader point: useful feedback tells learners what to do next. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. That explanation made later changes easier to discuss with residents and staff. For those taking part in feedback on a first essay, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
A useful plan for adult language learning must take account of the people who will use it. An idea may look complete on paper and still create difficulties during an ordinary week. Organizers therefore tried the adult language learning programme on a small scale and invited comments from users with different schedules. They recorded benefits as well as the time and resources needed to provide them. Some findings supported the original aim, while others suggested that the method should change. The group published both kinds of result instead of presenting the trial as a simple success or failure. This allowed residents to discuss the next step with a clearer understanding of its possible effects.
translation.explanation: 参考译文供考生自评，注意语义准确、逻辑关系及汉语通顺。
translation.referenceAnswer: 关于成人语言学习的有用方案必须考虑实际使用它的人。一个想法在纸上看似完整，平常使用时却仍可能出现困难。因此，组织者小规模试行该服务，并邀请时间安排不同的使用者提出意见。他们既记录益处，也记录提供这些益处所需的时间和资源。有些发现支持最初目标，另一些则表明方法应当调整。团队同时公布两类结果，而没有把试行简单说成成功或失败。这让居民能更清楚地了解可能的影响，再讨论下一步。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to the adult learning team about a community activity related to adult language learning. Explain how different people can participate, what should be recorded, and how the results should be shared.
writing.explanation: 范文供考生自评，注意任务要点、组织结构及语言准确性。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Committee Members,
I would like to propose a small improvement to the adult language learning programme. People have noticed speaking time concentrated among confident learners, and a short trial could help us understand how often this problem occurs. We should ask regular users and people who have not used the service before to describe their experiences. Their comments may reveal details that a plan made in an office would miss.
For one month, staff could keep a simple record of participation, time spent and any difficulties reported. We should also explain the purpose of the trial in clear language so that residents know how to contribute. After the month, please publish a brief summary of both benefits and limits. The final decision should be based on what people actually experienced, with a date for checking the arrangement again.
Yours sincerely,
A resident
